item.title: Kumamoto Art Museums near the Castle — Guide
item.description: In the castle district of central Kumamoto, close to the great fortress, art museums offer a refined cultural experience amid the city’s historic heart. Set near the Ōtemon (main gate) area and castle grounds, these galleries present a mix of modern and contemporary Japanese and Western art, works by artists connected to Kumamoto and the wider region, and changing special exhibitions, in calm, well-designed spaces. They provide an elegant contrast to the castle’s martial history and the greenery of its grounds, and are an ideal addition for visitors who enjoy art and want a quieter, indoor cultural stop between the castle, gardens and city sights.

item.title: Teshima Art Museum: A Space of Water and Light — Guide
item.description: The Teshima Art Museum, on the peaceful island of Teshima near Naoshima, is one of the most extraordinary museums in the world — though it contains just a single, endlessly changing work. Designed by architect Ryue Nishizawa with artist Rei Naito, the building is a vast, curving white concrete shell shaped like a water droplet, with two large oval openings to the sky. Inside there are no paintings or objects; instead, tiny droplets of water seep continuously from the floor, forming, merging, trickling and pooling in a slow, mesmerising dance, while wind, birdsong and light enter from above.

item.title: Tottori Prefectural Museum of Art — Guide
item.description: The Tottori Prefectural Museum of Art is the prefecture’s flagship art museum, a strikingly modern building in Kurayoshi in central Tottori that has quickly become a cultural anchor for the region. Its collection and changing exhibitions span the art of Tottori and the wider San’in region alongside modern and contemporary Japanese and international works, and its architecture — light-filled, open and designed as a public gathering space as much as a gallery — is part of the appeal.

item.title: Yufuin Art Museums & Galleries — Guide
item.description: Part of what gives Yufuin its distinctive artsy, upscale character is the cluster of small art museums and galleries scattered through the town, which set it apart from other hot-spring resorts. Along and just off the main street, visitors can discover an eclectic mix: elegant fine-art museums displaying Japanese and Western paintings, ceramics and sculpture, sometimes in beautiful garden settings; small private galleries and craft studios; and a range of quirky, fun themed museums that Yufuin is also known for.

item.title: Miho Museum: I.M. Pei's Shangri-La in the Shiga Mountains — Guide
item.description: The Miho Museum, designed by I.M. Pei — architect of the Louvre pyramid — is one of the world’s most theatrical museum arrivals: visitors walk or ride through a curving stainless-steel tunnel that opens onto a suspended bridge, the glass roofline of the museum appearing across the gorge like the hidden valley of Shangri-La that inspired it. To preserve the Shigaraki mountains, some 80% of the building is buried underground, its limestone-and-glass halls lit like a temple of light, and the collection matches the setting: superb antiquities from Egypt, Gandhara, Persia, China and Japan assembled by the Koyama family, joined by ambitious special exhibitions.

item.title: Fukui Prefectural Art Museum: Japanese and Regional Art in the City — Guide
item.description: The Fukui Prefectural Art Museum is a centrally located cultural stop in Fukui City, showcasing a collection of Japanese paintings, works by artists connected to the prefecture and rotating special exhibitions that change throughout the year. Its convenient location near Fukui Castle Ruins and the city centre makes it easy to combine with other central sights, offering an indoor cultural option that pairs well with an itinerary of the surrounding historical and civic attractions.

item.title: Omiya Bonsai Village: The Spiritual Home of Japanese Bonsai — Guide
item.description: Omiya Bonsai Village was founded in the 1920s when a group of Tokyo bonsai growers relocated here after the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake, seeking clean water and open land suited to cultivation. Today the neighbourhood remains the recognised spiritual home of Japanese bonsai, with several working nurseries open to visitors displaying trees, some centuries old, alongside the Omiya Bonsai Art Museum, the world’s first public museum dedicated entirely to the art form.
